messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Gary is a 53-year-old bus driver who has been with the same transit company for over twenty years. The rape happened on a cold November night near the end of a double shift. He had picked up a lone male passenger who seemed harmless enough—tired, like Gary himself—and then, somewhere along a dark stretch of suburban route, the man pulled a knife. The click of the blade locking open was the last sound Gary registered before everything narrowed to the confined space of the driver’s cabin, the weight of the man’s body, and the helplessness he had never known could live inside his own skin. He did not fight; he froze. Afterward, he drove the empty bus back to the depot, went home without a word, and showered for an hour.

In the weeks that followed, Gary tried to keep working, but the nightmares started immediately—not just images but the same visceral terror, the same suffocating shame, as if the event were still happening. The memory played like a film that would not stop, often triggered by ordinary moments: the exhaustion that settled into his bones at the end of a shift, the sudden presence of a passenger too close to his seat, the metallic clatter of a lunchbox or a dropped coin. Each time, the terror and shame rushed back. He came to believe that people could not be trusted—that any passenger might be a threat—and he lost whatever faith he had once had in the goodness of others. The shame attached itself to his body; he felt dirty, violated in a way that made him avoid his wife’s touch and dread changing clothes in the locker room.

Gary’s shifts became a minefield. When he felt tired, his vigilance dropped and a sudden sound could send him reeling into a full-blown memory replay, which in turn made him even more exhausted and hypervigilant. His negative beliefs fed this cycle: his mistrust made him scan every rider’s face for danger, and each time a trigger—a weary body, a crowded bus, an unexpected noise—confirmed his suspicion, deepening his sense that the world was unsafe and that his body had been permanently soiled. The memory itself became a trigger: replaying the rape made his ears strain for the sound of a blade, made him feel the fatigue of that night all over again, as if his body was trapped in a loop.

He started rearranging his schedule, taking only early-morning runs when the bus was half-empty, and he learned to avoid eye contact with passengers. If he felt exhaustion coming on, he would pull over, pretending to check the engine, just to get a moment alone. His wife noticed the distance; she thought he was having an affair. Gary could not tell her the truth—the shame was too great, and he was certain she would see him as weak or damaged. At work, his supervisor warned him about the unscheduled stops, but Gary could not explain.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a near-miss: he ran a red light during a brief dissociative episode triggered by a teenager laughing in the back—the pitch of the voice, he later realized, was a match. He pulled over, hands shaking, and sat in the driver’s seat until the next shift driver arrived. That night he told his wife he needed help, though he still could not name what happened. He is terrified of losing his job, of being seen as broken, and of the moment a therapist will ask him to describe that night in the bus. But he is more afraid of what might happen if he does not.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals (e.g., mistrust, shame, feeling soiled) causally lead to intrusive memories; negative beliefs are described as feeding a cycle but not directly triggering memory replays.
The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals causally lead to triggers; instead, triggers confirm negative appraisals, but appraisals are not shown to produce or amplify triggers themselves.
